chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Market Cycles, Era by Era

lessons.title: 2014 to Today: Reforms, Domestic Flows, and the SIP Era

body.text: The biggest change in Indian market cycles since 2014 is not a single reform or crash. It is who owns the market. Crores of Indians investing every month have made domestic money a counterweight to foreign selling. That has softened some falls. It has not abolished the cycle.

children.text: Every earlier lesson in this chapter covered an era that is over. This one covers the era you are investing in, which makes it both the most useful and the hardest to judge, because nobody yet knows how it ends. It runs from the 2014 election to mid 2025, and looks at three things: the reforms and shocks that reshaped the economy, the cycles that kept happening anyway, and the rise of domestic investors as the new force in Indian markets.

body.text: "Today" is a moving target. Figures in this lesson run to around mid 2025. Before relying on any number here, check the latest data on the NSE, AMFI and NSDL websites. Practising that habit is part of the lesson.

events.title: New government, new frameworks
events.description: A single-party majority government takes office. Jan Dhan accounts bring crores of households into the banking system. The RBI adopts inflation targeting, formalised in 2016 with a 4% CPI target and a band of 2% to 6%, and a Monetary Policy Committee. The EPFO begins investing part of its inflows in equities from 2015.

events.title: The bad loan reckoning
events.description: The RBI's Asset Quality Review forces banks to recognise hidden bad loans. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code arrives in 2016, and bank gross NPAs peak above 11% in March 2018.

events.title: Demonetisation and GST
events.description: ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, the large majority of currency in circulation by value, are withdrawn in November 2016, disrupting cash-based businesses. The Goods and Services Tax replaces a web of indirect taxes in July 2017. Both push more of the economy into the formal system, with short-term pain.

events.title: Credit accidents
events.description: The IL&FS default in 2018 triggers the NBFC crisis from Lesson 1.3. In March 2020 the RBI takes control of Yes Bank, which is rescued by an SBI-led group of lenders.

events.title: Corporate tax cut
events.description: The base corporate tax rate is cut from 30% to 22%, with 15% for new manufacturing companies. The Sensex jumps about 5% in a day.

events.title: COVID crash and recovery
events.description: The Nifty falls about 40% between January and March 2020, then recovers to a new high by November 2020 as the RBI cuts rates to 4% and floods the system with liquidity. A wave of new investors opens demat accounts.

events.title: Rate cycle and a capex revival
events.description: The RBI raises the repo rate from 4% to 6.5% between May 2022 and February 2023 to fight inflation. Government capital spending surges, bank NPAs fall below 3%, and rate cuts begin in February 2025, taking the repo rate to 5.5% by June 2025.

body.title: The SIP Era in One Number
body.prompt: The Nifty 50 closed near 7,200 in May 2014 and was around 25,000 roughly 11 years later. What was its CAGR over those 11 years, before dividends? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: Multiple = 25,000 ÷ 7,200 ≈ 3.47. CAGR = 3.47 to the power 1/11, minus 1 ≈ 12.0% a year. That is a strong result, and close to the index's long-run pace, but notice it arrived through four falls of 17% to 40%, not in a straight line. Add dividends of roughly 1% to 1.5% a year and the total return is a little higher.

markDefs.definition: Domestic institutional investors: Indian institutions that invest in the stock market, mainly mutual funds, insurance companies such as LIC, pension funds such as EPFO and NPS, and banks.
Foreign portfolio investors, earlier called foreign institutional investors: overseas funds and institutions that buy Indian shares and bonds, and can move money in and out quickly.

children.text: For most of India's market history, the swing factor was foreign money. Lessons 3.3 and 3.4 showed how FII inflows powered the 2003 to 2008 boom and how their exit deepened the 2008 crash and the 2013 taper tantrum. Since about 2016 a second force has grown to match them. Monthly SIPs, the AMFI "Mutual Funds Sahi Hai" campaign launched in 2017, EPFO equity investments, cheap discount brokers like Zerodha and the post-COVID rush of new investors have made

body.label: 2022: the year domestic money held the line
body.value: FPIs sold ~₹1.2 lakh crore of Indian shares. The Nifty still ended the year up about 4%.
body.context: Domestic institutions bought well over twice that amount. In the same year the US S&P 500 fell about 19%. In 2008, foreign selling of this scale would have meant a crash.

body.title: How the market's shock absorbers changed

columns.label: Foreign-flow era, 2003 to 2014
points: FII buying and selling set the direction of the market
Global risk-off events hit Indian shares and the rupee together
Retail investors mostly bought after rallies and sold after crashes
Domestic mutual funds too small to offset heavy foreign selling

columns.label: Domestic-flow era, 2016 onwards
points: Steady monthly SIP money arrives regardless of headlines
DIIs regularly absorb large foreign selling
Some drawdowns have been shallower and recoveries faster
But domestic money has also pushed some valuations, especially in mid and small caps, higher than foreign investors were willing to pay

body.title: What Changed, and What Didn't?
body.question: Which statement best describes the effect of rising domestic SIP and institutional flows on Indian market cycles?
options: They guarantee the Nifty can no longer fall more than 10%
They have made foreign selling less decisive and softened some falls, but they do not remove valuation, earnings or global risks, and they can slow down when returns disappoint
They have no effect, because only foreign investors move prices
They make valuations irrelevant, because money will always keep coming in
body.explanation: Domestic flows are a real structural change, visible in 2022 when heavy foreign selling did not cause a crash. But the March 2020 fall was still about 40%, and the Nifty fell about 17% from its September 2024 peak despite record SIP inflows. Flows also respond to returns: a long period of poor performance can slow SIP registrations and raise cancellations. Believing that flows make valuations irrelevant is a classic euphoria-stage idea.

body.text: Every boom in this course had a structural reason why this time was different: railways, the New Era of the 1920s, the Nifty Fifty, Japan's land, decoupling in 2007. "Domestic flows will always support the market" has the same shape. It contains real truth. It becomes dangerous when it is used to justify any price. SIP money is money from households who can pause, and have paused, when markets disappoint.

children.text: Signs of Excess in the SIP Era

body.caption: Late-cycle warning signs seen from 2023 to 2025, and how regulators responded

cells: Explosive growth in retail index options trading. A SEBI study found about 93% of individual F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24, with combined losses of about ₹1.8 lakh crore
SEBI raised minimum contract sizes and limited weekly expiries from late 2024
Tiny SME IPOs oversubscribed hundreds of times, as in Lesson 2.1, and heavy listing-day speculation
Exchanges and SEBI tightened SME listing rules and scrutiny
Rapid inflows into small cap funds and valuations well above historical averages
SEBI asked fund houses in 2024 to disclose stress tests showing how long it would take to sell small and mid cap holdings
Finfluencers on social media promoting trades and courses to first-time investors
SEBI restricted regulated entities from associating with unregistered finfluencers in 2024

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: A SEBI study found that about ___% of individual traders in equity F&O lost money between FY22 and FY24.
body.explanation: Roughly nine out of ten individual F&O traders lost money over those three years, with combined net losses of about ₹1.8 lakh crore. A surge in retail leverage of this kind is the same pattern as margin buying in the 1920s or part-paid railway shares in the 1840s.

body.title: Running a Cycle-Aware SIP
steps: Link each SIP to a specific goal and time horizon, and keep money needed within three years out of equities
Keep an emergency fund in a liquid fund or fixed deposit so you never have to stop an SIP or sell in a fall
Decide in advance that you will continue SIPs through a 20% to 40% fall, since every decade in this course has had one
Review your asset allocation once a year and rebalance, rather than reacting to headlines
Be wary of shifting SIPs into whichever category did best last year, especially small caps or thematic funds after big rallies
Keep leverage, including F&O and loans against securities, out of your long-term plan

body.title: "India Can't Crash Anymore"
body.scenario: Your 27-year-old friend in Pune opened a Zerodha account in 2021. Apart from a few short dips, she has only seen markets rise. She tells you: "SIP money comes in every month no matter what, so the Nifty can't have a 2008-style crash anymore. I've moved all my savings, including my emergency fund, into small cap funds, and I trade options on weekly expiry to boost returns."
body.prompt: Using the whole of Chapter 3, what is right about her view, what is wrong, and what would you suggest?
body.modelAnswer: She is right that something important has changed. Domestic flows are now large enough to absorb heavy foreign selling, as 2022 showed, and some recent falls have been shallower and shorter than in 2008 or the 1990s. But she has only lived through one part of the cycle, which is exactly how investors were conditioned in 2004 to 2007 and in 1982 to 2000. The Nifty still fell about 40% in 2020, and about 17% from September 2024 to April 2025, despite record SIP inflows, and small caps usually fall considerably more than the Nifty. SIP money comes from households who can pause when they are scared or need cash. And several signs from this lesson's excess table, heavy retail options trading, stretched small cap valuations and IPO frenzies, are the kind that tend to appear late in a cycle, not early. Her own plan concentrates three risks: no emergency fund, so any job loss or medical need could force her to sell at a bad time; everything in the most volatile part of the market; and weekly options, where SEBI's own data shows about nine in ten individual traders lost money. A cycle-aware version would rebuild an emergency fund first, spread her equity SIPs across large, mid and small caps in line with her goals, and treat options trading, if at all, as a small amount she can afford to lose.

cards.definition: Domestic institutional investor: Indian mutual funds, insurers, pension funds and banks investing in the market.
Foreign portfolio investor: an overseas investor in Indian shares and bonds, the successor term to FII.
The RBI's framework since 2016 of aiming for 4% CPI inflation within a band of 2% to 6%, with rates set by a Monetary Policy Committee.
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code of 2016, which created a time-bound process to resolve failed companies and helped clean up bank balance sheets.
The steady buying by SIP investors and DIIs that has offset foreign selling since about 2016. It softens falls but does not make valuations irrelevant.
SEBI's 2024 finding that about 93% of individual F&O traders lost money from FY22 to FY24, which led to tighter derivatives rules.

body.label: NSE: Market Pulse
body.description: NSE's monthly Market Pulse report, available on its website, tracks new investor registrations, ownership of listed companies by DIIs and FPIs, and market valuations. It is the easiest way to update the figures in this lesson.

children.text: That completes India's market history, from banyan trees to crores of demat accounts. So far this course has focused on equities. Chapter 4 widens the lens to the cycles that drive them from outside: commodity supercycles in oil, gold and metals, RBI interest rate cycles and bond yields, and the rotation of sector leadership from one Indian market era to the next.

body.text: Index levels, flows, account numbers and other figures in this lesson are approximate, rounded and current only to around mid 2025, and may since have changed. Nothing here is a forecast, a recommendation to buy or sell any security, or investment advice. F&O trading carries a high risk of loss. Consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own situation.

points: From 2014 to 2025, inflation targeting, the IBC, GST, the bank clean-up and a corporate tax cut rewired the economy, alongside shocks from demonetisation, the NBFC crisis and COVID
Cycles did not stop: the Nifty fell about 25% in 2015 to 2016, 40% in 2020, 18% in 2021 to 2022 and 17% in 2024 to 2025, yet still grew about 12% a year from 2014
Domestic money became a new shock absorber: demat accounts rose from about 4 crore in 2020 to about 19 crore in 2025, and DIIs overtook FPIs in ownership of NSE-listed companies in early 2025
In 2022, FPIs sold about ₹1.2 lakh crore of shares but the Nifty still ended the year up about 4%, something unthinkable in the foreign-flow era
Domestic flows soften falls but do not remove valuation, earnings or global risk, and "flows will always support the market" has the shape of every past this-time-is-different story
Late-cycle signs such as heavy retail F&O losses, SME IPO frenzies and stretched small cap valuations appeared from 2023 to 2025, prompting SEBI to tighten rules
